  - remove that attention and check whether the B nets lose their sign dependence (and what it costs them).
  This would be the first route-level account of what distinguishes the two solution types.

## Update 43 (2026-10-30 00:03Z): E34, B nets' block-2 query attends three times more to the labelled tokens than A nets'; that path reproduces about a third of B's negation shift (amendment 42)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (path patching with real counterfactual states; the coordinator's suggestion).** In the 48 acquired clean nets, on 3,000 bases of E28's data, for each base and each of its eight negation patterns (all with the same Bayes posterior), at block 2's query row:
  - path: the labelled tokens' keys and values come from the negated pattern, everything else from the base;
  - rev: the reverse.
  The head reads only the query token, so this is the route by which the labelled tokens' block-1 states reach the output in block 2. Swapping keys also changes the softmax weights on the other tokens.
- **The path reproduces about a third of B's negation shift (P160 fails on its registered mean-shift criterion).**
  - Projected on the true single-source negation shift of the predictive mean, the path hybrid reproduces 0.31 of it in the B bases (bar ≥ 0.5), and restoring the path alone removes 0.29.
  - These are projections. The hybrid also moves the mean in other directions: in mix4_s4 its squared shift is 4.5× the true one.
  - P160's second criterion, path-only cost ≥ 0.5 × full cost, is met numerically (2.82). But the hybrid families double the B nets' KL (path-only ×1.98, all-but-path ×2.05), so these costs are unsuitable as an intrinsic share of the natural sign dependence.
- **In A the path reproduces less (P161 holds).** Projection 0.12 in the A bases (bar ≤ 0.3 and below B). The A nets' family-mean KL changes by less than 3% under the hybrids.
- **Where block 2's query attends (descriptive).**
  - A bases: 83% on the three summary tokens, 13% on the twelve labelled tokens.
  - B bases: 53% on the summaries, 41% on the labelled tokens.
  - Post hoc, per base, the labelled-token mass is 0.06-0.28 in A and 0.39-0.45 in B, and the projection share is 0.08-0.17 in A and 0.24-0.42 in B: no overlap on either.
- **What this says.**
  - Both groups' block-2 query reads mostly the summaries; B nets also give the labelled tokens three times as much attention.
  - Isolated, that route reproduces about a third of B's negation shift, as a projection.
  - B nets are also much more sensitive to hybrids that mix states from two sign patterns.
  - Where the rest of B's sign dependence enters, and what B's block 2 computes from the labelled tokens, are not identified.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for three fixes, all done (`results/review_e34.md`):
  - treat the shares as projections, without attributing the remainder to the summaries;
  - describe the attention and the disruption as sensitivity, with the consistency and E7 readings as hypotheses;
  - qualify the cost criterion rather than call it unusable.
  It confirmed the hybrids, the pooling, P160-P161 as registered and the per-base table.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

## Update 46 (2026-10-30 01:43Z): E30, retraining with invariant input formats; the sign-free format cuts the KL to between a third and a half of the control's (amendment 38)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** The tiny-pfn recipe (2 layers, width 32, mixture head) was trained from scratch on one L4 GPU in four input-format arms, seeds 0-11 each:
  - ctrl: the original format;
  - mag: labelled readings y + |o − y|, so the labelled errors carry no sign;
  - sgnmag: the original signed readings plus a feature |o − y|, the coordinator's representation control;
  - fix: fixed identity codes.
  KL is the test gap in each net's own format.
- **Pairing.** ctrl, mag and fix share each seed's initialisation and episode stream. sgnmag does not share the initialisation: its extra input feature changes the first layer's size, which shifts every later random draw. The registration's statement that every arm shares the initialisation is wrong for sgnmag. Episode streams start the same in every arm, but nets stop at different steps (50k or 90k).
- **Results.** Two summaries, which differ: per-arm means over each arm's acquired nets (gap < 0.10), and paired ratios on seeds acquired in both arms, with 2,000 bootstrap resamples of those seeds.

| arm | acquired | mean KL | median KL | ratio of arm means to ctrl | paired ratio to ctrl [95% CI] (seeds) | A / B types |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ctrl | 11 of 12 | 0.0129 | 0.0104 | 1 | 1 | 4 / 7 |
| mag | 12 of 12 | 0.0061 | 0.0045 | 0.47 | 0.36 [0.27, 0.49] (11) | 11 / 1 |
| sgnmag (not paired at initialisation) | 10 of 12 | 0.0087 | 0.0056 | 0.67 | 0.66 [0.36, 1.30] (9) | 7 / 3 |
| fix | 12 of 12 | 0.0064 | 0.0064 | 0.49 | 0.48 [0.34, 0.73] (11) | 4 / 8 |

- **The sign-free format gains much more than the measured sign cost (P150 fails, high).**
  - The ctrl nets' sign-flip KL reduction (a nine-draw geometric-averaging measure on separate data) is 0.20 [0.15, 0.25] of their KL, so the registered band for the KL reduction was 0.10-0.30.
  - The paired reduction is 0.64 [0.50, 0.73]; the arm-mean reduction is 0.53. Descriptively, the paired reduction is about 3.2 times that benchmark.
  - Every paired seed improves: B-type ctrl seeds by 1.8-5.4×, A-type seeds by 1.3-2.3×. The mean paired reductions are 0.0115 and 0.0026 nats (P153 holds).
  - 11 of 12 mag nets are A type (middle-range rom < 0), against 4 of 11 ctrl nets. Their large-range rom (big-miss departure) is 0.083 against 0.141.
- **With the magnitude given, the signs are almost dropped (P151 fails on its KL part).**
  - The sgnmag nets' sign-flip reduction is 1.3% of their KL against 19.9% in ctrl (P151's second part holds).
  - Their KL is 1.31× mag's on the paired seeds [0.64, 2.54] and 1.42× on arm means (bar ≤ 1.1). The interval includes 1.1.
  - 3 of 10 acquired sgnmag nets are B type with KL 0.009-0.022; the A-type ones have 0.0041-0.0079, close to mag (0.0034-0.0068). Two seeds stalled.
- **Fixed codes halve the KL (P152 holds).**
  - The paired reduction is 0.52 [0.28, 0.66], against the registered half of the code-averaging cost (0.5 × 0.28).
  - The fix nets' KL is 0.67 [0.49, 0.94] of the code-averaged ctrl KL, so fixing the codes gains more than averaging over them. Fixing them also removes the question-code variation and may make binding easier; neither is separated here.
  - Most fix nets are "B" by the middle-range sign (8 of 12), yet their KL and sign cost are low, so this diagnostic does not mean the same thing in every format.
- **Cost:** one on-demand L4 for 2.26 h, about $1.97 at the rate ceiling (rate unverified); lane total about $3.07 of $40.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e30.md`):
  - disclose sgnmag's unpaired initialisation;
  - report both the arm-mean and the paired summaries;
  - keep solution-selection and easier binding as hypotheses;
  - call the threefold figure a descriptive ratio to a finite-ensemble benchmark;
  - correct the per-seed improvement range.
  It confirmed the format implementations, the evaluation routing, every ctrl-mag seed improving, P150-P153 as recorded and the GPU accounting.

| seed | ctrl | type | mag | seed | ctrl | type | mag |

**What this says.**
- **In this recipe the input format changes the attained distance from Bayes by a factor of two to three.** Removing the signs that Bayes ignores cuts the KL to between a third (paired) and a half (arm means) of the control's. That is much more than the sign dependence measured on trained ctrl nets. The A/B diagnostic also shifts almost entirely to A.
  - A candidate explanation, untested: access to the signs lets training settle on B-type solutions with larger errors, so removing the signs changes which solution training finds, not just whether a sign term is present.
- **Given the magnitude, nets nearly stop using the signs, but some still end in high-error B-type solutions.** sgnmag's initialisation differs from the other arms', so this comparison is less clean.
- **Fixed codes also roughly halve the KL.** How much of that is invariance, easier binding or the removed question-code variation is not separated.
- **For M2.**
  - This is the first result in this program that changes the architecture's input to remove what the posterior ignores and measures the effect by retraining.
  - The effect is large, and larger than the measured invariance costs. So invariance costs measured on a trained net underestimate the gain from building the invariance in.
  - Generalising beyond this world and recipe needs new tests.
- **Limits.**
  - One world and one recipe, with 12 seeds per arm.
  - sgnmag is not paired at initialisation.
  - The A/B diagnostic is a middle-range derivative sign whose meaning varies with the format.
  - The mag format also changes the input distribution: all residuals are non-negative.

## Update 47 (2026-10-30 03:09Z): E41, the single-source pooling toy depends on the signs, but a sign-free input does not help it; format switches show an asymmetric path dependence (amendment 49)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** E20's 'ln' toy (one source's four labelled errors; linear token embedding, LayerNorm, one learned-query attention pool, readout MLP to the posterior over the three noise levels), 12 seeds per arm, the same initialisation and episodes per seed in every arm:
  - ctrl (signed errors) and mag (o = y + |r|): 24,000 constant-lr steps, then a 6,000-step cooldown;
  - c2m2k, c2m12k: ctrl, then mag after 2,000 or 12,000 steps (same schedule);
  - m2c12k: mag, then ctrl after 12,000 steps;
  - mag18: mag with c2m12k's post-switch budget (12,000 + 6,000 steps).
  KL to the exact level posterior on one set of 20,000 fresh episodes, in the final format.
- **The toy depends on the signs (P176 holds).** Geometric averaging over the base and 8 sign patterns removes 8.8% [7.6%, 10.1%] of the family's mean KL in the ctrl toys (uncorrected); averaging over the base and its negation (all four errors reversed) removes 8.3%.
- **A sign-free input does not help it (P177 fails).** The mag toys end at 0.00059 nats against ctrl's 0.00053: rho = 1 - K_mag/K_ctrl = -0.11 [-0.15, -0.07] (registered bar: rho >= 1.5 x c_sign). mag is above ctrl in 11 of 12 seeds. Within each arm, the 12 seeds lie within ±14% of the arm mean.
- **The registered lock-in test loses its meaning here (P178 fails as registered).** R divides by K_ctrl - K_mag, which is negative, so its values (c2m2k -1.99, c2m12k -3.57, mag18 2.45) do not measure rescue. Directly:
  - c2m12k ends at 0.00032 and c2m2k at 0.00041 (mag format), below both pure arms in every seed;
  - m2c12k ends at 0.00068 (ctrl format), above ctrl in every seed and close to mag18 (0.00067).
- **Early learning (descriptive).** mag acquires much faster (median KL at 1,000 steps 0.0056 against ctrl's 0.187; at 3,000 steps 0.0032 against 0.0057); by 12,000 steps the two are close (0.0022 and 0.0024); the cooldown lowers both three- to fivefold.
- **What it shows.** In this toy the signed format slows acquisition and leaves a 9% sign cost, yet ctrl training ends at least as well as mag training, and ctrl training followed by mag ends best. Starting with mag and switching to ctrl leaves a worse solution than ctrl from the start. So the toy has path dependence in both directions under this finite budget, but this toy under this recipe does not reproduce E30's final sign-free gain (3.2 times the sign cost in the full nets). The merge of several sources in block 2, where the full nets' A/B types differ, is one untested candidate for what produces it.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e41.md`):
  - state that this toy under this recipe does not reproduce the gain, without claiming that the multi-source structure is necessary;
  - drop the claim that the toy has no solution types (the A/B diagnostic was not measured; a narrow KL spread does not exclude them) and an incorrect comparison with E30;
  - say that the intervals are over training seeds, conditional on one shared evaluation set;
  - remove a loosely argued LayerNorm explanation of the order effect;
  - describe the costs as shares of the family's mean KL, and the negation cost as averaging over the base and its negation.
  It confirmed the formats, the paired initialisation and episodes, the switch timing and schedules, the exact posterior and its sign invariance, the KL and cost formulas, the tables and P176-P178 as registered.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

**What this says.**
- **This toy does not reproduce the amplified sign-free gain.** The toy keeps the step where E24-E25 located the big-miss contrast (a source's own pooling of normalised token features), and it depends on the signs, but removing them does not lower its final KL. One architecture, target and schedule cannot show what the full nets need for their 2-3x gain (E30); the multi-source merge is one untested candidate.
- **The toy has path dependence, in a direction we did not expect.** Signed training followed by sign-free training ends best; the reverse ends worst; both relative to the pure arms in every seed. Why the order matters is not tested.
- **For M2.** The sign dependence appears in a model with only the pooling step; the large retraining gain does not. E37 (format switches in the full nets) tests whether the full nets' gain reflects a lock-in.
- **Limits.** One toy architecture and schedule; the toy's KL is about 20 times smaller than the full nets'; the toy predicts the noise level, not y*; one shared evaluation set.

## Update 48 (2026-10-30 05:20Z): E40, a second world: the nets depend on the per-example signs (about a third of their KL), but the gain from a sign-free format did not follow from that cost (amendment 48)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** A second world (`t2_world.py`): in-context linear regression with an unknown noise level (w ~ N(0, I_D); noise variance 0.1, 0.5 or 2.0; eight examples and a query; exact Bayes is a three-component mixture, exactly invariant under flipping any example (x_i, y_i) -> (-x_i, -y_i)). pfn2's set transformer (2 layers, width 32, 2 heads, mixture head K = 4), the fixed 90,000-step schedule, seeds 0-11 with the same initialisation and episodes in both formats:
  - ctrl: tokens [x_i, y_i, 0];
  - canon: each example replaced by its flip-orbit representative with y_i >= 0 (x_i co-flipped), so the input is exactly flip-invariant.
  D = 2 (primary) and D = 1. One on-demand L4, 2.31 h, about $2.01.
- **The nets depend on the per-example signs (P174 holds).** In ctrl nets, geometric averaging over the base and 8 random flip patterns removes 34% [30%, 38%] of the family's mean KL at D = 2 (per seed 24-43%) and 32% at D = 1 (27-37%); in the first world it was about 20% (E30's ctrl nets). Averaging over the base and its joint negation removes 15% (D = 2) and 17% (D = 1).
- **The format gain did not follow from that cost (P175 fails narrowly at D = 2; no detectable mean gain at D = 1).**
  - D = 2: the canonical format halves the KL (ctrl 0.0187, canon 0.0092 nats; rho = 1 - K_canon/K_ctrl = 0.51 [0.42, 0.58]); every seed improves (canon/ctrl 0.34-0.81). That is 1.49 times the sign cost on the same seeds, just under the registered bar of 1.5 (P175 requires >= 1.5 x c_sign and rho >= 0.1); a joint bootstrap of rho - 1.5 x c_sign gives -0.002 [-0.12, 0.11] (post-review check), so the result is indistinguishable from the bar.
  - D = 1: no gain (ctrl 0.0032, canon 0.0033; rho = -0.03 [-0.24, 0.14]; 5 seeds improve, 7 worsen), although the ctrl nets' sign cost is 32% of their KL.
- **Learning speed (descriptive, validation curves).** At D = 2 the canonical nets are ahead at every step (median validation gap at 20,000 steps 0.040 against 0.053; at 80,000, 0.023 against 0.036); at D = 1 only slightly, early.
- **What it shows.** The invariance failure carries over to a world with a different structure (one regression problem, exchangeable examples, no labels or identity codes), at an even larger share of the KL. E30's 3.2-fold gain was not reproduced: D = 2 narrowly misses the registered 1.5-fold criterion and D = 1 shows no detectable mean gain. With E41's toy (no gain at a 9% cost), the four settings measured so far give retraining gains from below zero to 3.2 times the measured cost (finite-ensemble benchmarks), so in these settings the cost measured on trained nets did not predict what building the invariance into the input gains.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for three fixes, all done (`results/review_e40.md`; checks in `e40_post.py`, `results/e40_post.json`):
  - state that E30's magnitude was not reproduced, that D = 2 narrowly misses the bar and D = 1 shows no detectable mean gain, and restrict the conclusion to these settings; bootstrap the margin rho - 1.5 x c_sign jointly (done);
  - say "halves the mean KL; all 12 seeds improve" rather than halving for every net;
  - compare the canonical nets and the sign-averaged ctrl predictions on identical episodes with the same estimator before ordering them (done), and drop the causal attribution.
  It confirmed the Bayes predictive and its flip invariance, the canonicalisation and pairing, the grid coverage, the costs, the acquisition rule, the tables and P174-P175 as registered.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

| # | test | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| P174 | D = 2: c_sign >= 0.05 | holds: 0.341 |
| P175 | D = 2: rho >= 1.5 x c_sign and rho >= 0.1 | fails narrowly: rho 0.51, 1.5 x c_sign = 0.512; the intervals overlap the bar |

**What this says.**
- **The sign-invariance failure is not specific to the first world.** In a regression world with exchangeable examples and no identity codes, the nets' predictions depend on per-example signs that Bayes ignores, at about a third of their KL. This is the first cross-task support for the invariance part of the account.
- **The retraining gain is a separate quantity.** Building the invariance into the input gained 3.2 times the measured cost in the first world (E30), about 1.5 times here at D = 2, nothing detectable at D = 1, and less than nothing in E41's toy. On identical episodes and with the same estimator (post-review check):
  - D = 1: the canonical nets' KL is 0.0029, equal to the ctrl nets' 0.0029, while the ctrl nets' sign-averaged predictions reach 0.0019; the canonical net is below them in 1 of 12 seeds. Training on sign-free inputs did not reach the invariant predictor that averaging the ctrl nets gives; why is not tested.
  - D = 2: the canonical nets (0.0088) are below the sign-averaged ctrl predictions (0.0117) in 8 of 12 seeds.
- **For M2.** "Small transformers fail to learn posterior invariances that act on individual inputs" now holds in two worlds. "Building such an invariance in removes more than its measured cost" held strongly only in the first world, where the format also changes the A/B solution type (E30); in these other settings it did not. E37 tests whether the first world's gain is a lock-in.
- **Limits.** One architecture and schedule; two input dimensions; 12 seeds per cell; the canonical map (y >= 0) is one of several possible representatives.

## Update 49 (2026-10-30 06:40Z): E37, the format-switch test: removing the signs late rescues most B seeds, against the registered selection predictions; a late reverse switch is harmful (amendment 45)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (the coordinator's switch test).** The tiny-pfn recipe (2 layers, width 32, mixture head) with a fixed 90,000-step schedule, seeds 0-11, the same initialisation and episodes per seed in all 11 arms:
  - ctrl and mag (signs removed from the labelled errors) throughout;
  - ctrl then mag after K = 2k, 3k, 6k, 10k or 30k steps (c2mK);
  - mag then ctrl after 3k, 10k or 30k (m2cK);
  - mag60: mag with 60,000 steps, the budget c2m30k has after its switch.
  R(arm) = sum (K_ctrl - K_arm) / sum (K_ctrl - K_mag) over the 11 seeds acquired in ctrl, mag and the arm: 1 = as good as mag from scratch, 0 = as ctrl. Seed 3's ctrl net stalled, as in E30.
- **Checks.** The ctrl and mag nets reproduce E30's 90,000-step nets exactly (identical validation curves; test-gap difference 0), and every switched net equals its parent arm at the switch step (96 checkpoint pairs, difference 0).
- **The registered selection predictions miss their bars (P166-P170 fail as scored; several intervals cross the bars).**
  - A late switch rescues most of the gap: R(c2m30k) = 0.70 [0.46, 0.97] (bar <= 0.5); R(c2m10k) 0.70, R(c2m6k) 0.73, R(c2m3k) 0.75. mag60 reaches 0.86 [0.74, 0.94].
  - An early switch rescues less than predicted: R(c2m2k) = 0.48 [-0.05, 0.97] (bar >= 0.8); seeds 7 and 8 end with high KL.
  - The late-switched nets' block-2 attention to the labelled tokens moves about halfway toward mag's: Rlab(c2m30k) = 0.53 [0.37, 0.71] (bar <= 0.5; mean lab: ctrl 0.301, c2m30k 0.205, mag 0.150).
  - Only 1 of the 7 B-type seeds is still B after the 30k switch (bar: at least half); 2 of 7 after the 2k switch (bar: at most a quarter).
  - The reverse switch makes nets worse than ctrl: R(m2c10k) = -0.33 [-1.47, 0.22], R(m2c30k) = -0.68 [-1.98, -0.02] (bar >= 0.5).
- **Per seed (post hoc, `e37_post.py`).** Without seed 8, R is 0.91-0.97 for every switch from 3k to 30k. Seed 8's switched nets all end at KL 0.026-0.028 and B type (its mag net reaches 0.0042). Seed 3, stalled in ctrl, ends at KL 0.0037-0.0040 after a switch at 2-6k, acquired but at 0.029 after the 10k switch, and still unacquired after the 30k switch. The c2m nets end below mag60 in 7-9 of 11 seeds, while mag60's pooled R (0.86) is above c2m30k's (0.70), mainly because of seed 8.
- **Trajectories (descriptive; medians over seeds).**
  - At the 3,000-step checkpoint (the first rom checkpoint; median KL 0.13 in ctrl, 0.07 in mag) every net in every arm has a positive middle-range rom (B), in both formats. Without signs the B share falls to 0.33 by 10,000 steps and 0.08 at the end; with signs to 0.92 at 10,000 and 0.67 from 30,000 on.
  - ctrl to mag at 30k: KL (format in force) 0.033 at 30,000, 0.027 250 steps later; the B share falls from 0.67 to 0.17-0.25 over the next 30,000-60,000 steps.
  - mag to ctrl at 30k: KL jumps from 0.017 to 0.078 within 250 steps (to 0.099 from 0.033 for the 10k switch); the B share is 0.92 by 35,000 and stays there; block-2 attention to the labelled tokens rises from 0.12 to 0.36. The m2c10k and m2c30k nets' sign-flip cost is 32-33% of their KL (ctrl 20%).
- **What it shows.**
  - Under this recipe and budget, for 6 of 7 B-type seeds the signed format's cost was not locked in: removing the signs at 3,000-30,000 steps brought them to mag-level KL and the A type. A hypothesis that fits: the cost is paid while the signs are visible.
  - At the first type checkpoint (3,000 steps) every net looks B; without signs most stop looking B within about 10,000 steps, with signs only some do, and putting the signs back after 10,000-30,000 mag steps returns nets to B. If the signs hold nets in the B state, E30's gain exceeding the measured sign cost would follow, because the B state's extra error is larger than its sign dependence; this is an interpretation, not a test.
  - Exceptions persist through the tested budget: seed 8 after every switch from 2,000 steps on, and seed 3 after the 10,000- and 30,000-step switches.
  - To the coordinator's question: late-switched, sign-free nets keep about half of the B-like block-2 attention mass on the labelled tokens (0.205 against 0.301 in ctrl and 0.150 in mag) while their KL and type are mag-like. Attention mass is descriptive, so this shows only that the retained attention coexists with a mag-like KL.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e37.md`):
  - report that the registered predictions miss their bars, with intervals that cross them, and keep the mechanism a hypothesis;
  - drop "permanent" for seed 3 and seed 8 (acquired but high-error at 10k; unacquired at 30k; persistence only through the tested budget);
  - describe the type at the first sampled checkpoint (3,000 steps), not "at acquisition", and the routing result as descriptive coexistence;
  - call mag60 a remaining-step-budget control;
  - restrict the six-of-seven rescue to switches at 3k-30k and the reverse-switch harm to 10k and 30k.
  It confirmed the switch, the schedule, the paired initialisation, the final-format evaluation, model selection, the filtering, the R and Rlab rules, the bootstrap, the tables, the reproduction of E30's curves, the branch-point checks and the P166-P170 scoring.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

**What this says.**
- **The registered selection account is not supported.** The coordinator's question was whether the solution is chosen early and then kept. For 6 of the 7 B-type seeds it was not: after the signs were removed, even at 30,000 steps, they reached mag-level KL and the A type. The predictions were scored as registered on point estimates, and the late-switch interval reaches down to 0.46, so this is a failure of the registered bars rather than a statistical rejection; per seed the picture is clear. That E30's gain is an ongoing effect of visible signs is the reading that fits, not a tested mechanism.
- **Path dependence remains, in the other direction.** A net that learned without signs for 10,000-30,000 steps and then sees them ends worse than one that saw them from the start, and more sign-dependent (the 3,000-step reverse switch ends between the two, R = 0.34). The toy of E41 showed the same asymmetry.
- **Some seeds stay bad through the tested budget, not in the predicted pattern.** Seed 8 is bad after any switch from 2,000 steps on; seed 3 is high-error after the 10,000-step switch and unacquired after the 30,000-step one; seed 7 is bad only after the 2,000-step switch.
- **For M2 ("how they learn"), as a hypothesis.** The A/B split looks like a transition out of a B state that every net shows at the first checkpoint: visible signs would inhibit it, removing them would release it, and reintroducing them would reverse it. E43 tests what decides, under the signs, which nets make the transition.
- **Limits.** 11 usable seeds, R pooled as a ratio of sums and dominated by the B seeds; one recipe and schedule; mag60 controls the remaining step budget only (it also has a fresh optimiser state, warmup and other episodes), so it does not exclude slower adaptation after a switch; the type diagnostic (middle-range rom sign) behaves differently across formats (E30), and the first type checkpoint is at 3,000 steps; attention masses are descriptive; the trajectory measures are medians on 4,000 test episodes.

One on-demand L4, 3.90 h, about $3.39.
- **P171 fails as registered (width 64).**
  - rho: width 32 0.69 [0.54, 0.78]; width 64 0.18 [-0.39, 0.60]; width 128 0.62 [0.50, 0.71]; depth 3 0.57 [0.36, 0.76].
  - Width 64 is heterogeneous: 3 of its 10 mag nets (seeds 4, 5 and 7) ended B type with KL 0.019-0.020, above their ctrl twins; the other 7 are at 0.19-0.74 of their ctrl twins. These three nets are part of the registered estimand. Under the amendment's wording, P171's failure would mean that capacity learns the invariance; the width-64 data do not show that either, because the failure comes from sign-free nets ending in B, not from ctrl nets dropping their sign dependence.
  - Post hoc, two median-based summaries over the paired seeds: the ratio of median mag KL to median ctrl KL is 0.36 (width 32), 0.40 (64), 0.33 (128) and 0.47 (depth 3); the median of the per-seed ratios is 0.34, 0.45, 0.47 and 0.54.

- **KL by size.** Mean KL ctrl: 0.0127 (width 32), 0.0097 (64), 0.0072 (128), 0.0100 (depth 3; median 0.0063); mag: 0.0055, 0.0080 (median 0.0037), 0.0027, 0.0043. Median KL falls with width in both formats; the mean mag KL is worse at width 64 because of the three B nets.
- **The sign-cost share does not shrink with width.** The ctrl nets' sign-flip cost (the KL reduction of nine-draw geometric averaging, on separate data) is 20% of their KL at width 32, 24% at 64, 25% at 128, and 15% at depth 3. B types among the ctrl nets: 7 of 11, 8 of 10, 6 of 10, 6 of 10. The last block's query attention to the labelled tokens in ctrl nets rises with width (0.30, 0.47, 0.49; depth 3, block 3: 0.39).
- **What it shows.** At width 128 and at depth 3 the sign-free format still lowers the mean KL by about 60% under this budget, and signed nets keep a sign-cost share of 15-25% at every size tried; at width 64 the outcome is heterogeneous and the registered test fails. Post hoc, the typical (median) net gains at every size. So these data show no sign that the gap closes with capacity up to width 128, but they do not establish that it is an architectural inevitability; the pooling-order prediction for depth failed in this cohort. At width 64 some sign-free nets also ended B, so the B solution is not produced by visible signs alone.

## Update 54 (2026-10-30 07:47Z): E45, single-pass LLM answers are not sign-invariant; without the stated model they move like a correction for a source's mean error, with it no pooled correction is detected (amendment 53)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** E18's 60 base episodes; in each, the source with the largest |mean error| (median |mean error| 0.65) has its four displayed errors negated, which leaves Bayes unchanged. Stated (generative model given) and unstated ("forecasters") framings. Single-pass answers (one number, no reasoning): Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.8 with thinking off, GPT-5.6 at reasoning "none" (two samples per prompt), local Qwen3-1.7B (greedy). Per pair: the shift D = answer(negated) - answer(original); X = 2 x mean error x Bayes weight of that source, the weight being the local derivative of the Bayes mean with respect to the source's reading; a correction that subtracts the mean error at that weight gives D = c X with c = 1 (an operational, linearised scale, not general Bayesian debiasing). Invariance ratio = mean D^2 / retest variance (about 1 if the answers ignore the signs). Claude spend $4.14 at list price (cap $6).
- **Stated framing: no pooled bias correction detected (P187 fails).** The pooled slope over the three Claude arms is 0.06 [-0.31, 0.32]. Per model (intervals unadjusted, descriptive): Haiku 0.53 [0.23, 0.81], Opus 0.08 [-0.07, 0.26], Sonnet -0.44 [-1.28, 0.19]; GPT 0.08 [-0.09, 0.35].
  - Invariance ratios: Opus 2.81 [1.50, 4.63], robust to leaving out any one pair (2.40-3.15); Haiku 2.09 [0.84, 4.59]; GPT 0.92 [0.42, 2.62]; Sonnet 7.41 [1.55, 26.2], but fragile: one pair with single answers carries 65% of its squared shifts, and on the 56 pairs with all four answers the ratio is 2.26 and the slope -0.20 (post-review check).
- **Unstated framing: answers move like a bias correction (P188 holds on its point estimate).** Pooled Claude slope 1.20 [0.24, 1.86] (bar >= 0.5; the interval extends below 0.5): Haiku 0.28 [-0.20, 0.88], Opus 0.50 [0.13, 0.84], Sonnet 2.83 [0.26, 4.71]; GPT 1.42 [0.19, 2.46] (one pair carries 59% of GPT's squared shifts; leaving out one pair gives 0.58-1.51). Invariance ratios 1.6-3.4.
- **Accuracy.** Mean absolute deviation from Bayes: 0.12-0.22 (stated) and 0.25-0.55 (unstated) for the Claude and GPT arms; Qwen3-1.7B 4.7-7.7, too inaccurate to interpret.
- **What it shows.** Single-pass LLM answers were not invariant to the signs of a source's past errors in this task. Without the generative model, the dependence is compatible with a familiar heuristic, subtracting a source's average past error as a bias, which is sensible for real forecasters. With the model stated, no pooled correction was detected, Opus still changed its answers with the signs beyond its retest noise without a detected proportional direction, and Haiku corrected partly. The small nets' sign dependence was not the registered proportional correction (E28); whether the two arise from different mechanisms is not established here.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e45.md`; checks in `e45_post.py`, `results/e45_post.json`):
  - add complete-four-answer and leave-one-pair-out sensitivities and qualify Sonnet's invariance result (done: 2.26 on complete pairs; one pair carries 65%);
  - describe compatibility with a bias-correction heuristic, without claiming learned priors or a reasoning effect (E18 used other models and manipulations);
  - define the slope's scale as operational (local weights);
  - say "not detected" for nulls, name the Claude pool, call per-arm intervals unadjusted, and note that P188 passes on its point estimate;
  - correct presentation details (Qwen one sample, the stated deviation range 0.12-0.22, "no reasoning" requested rather than verified for GPT, the Bayes answer under the stated model).
  It confirmed the 60 negations and Bayes equalities, the hashes, E18b's settings, parsing, retries and filtering, the formulas, the tables, P187-P188 and the spend ($4.14).
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

**What this says.**
- **LLMs did not ignore the signs either.** In a single pass, the models' answers moved when a source's past errors were reversed, which Bayes under the stated model ignores. Given only "forecasters", their answers moved like a correction for the average past error, about one unit on our linearised scale on average, with large model differences (Sonnet's slope 2.8). With the zero-mean model stated, no pooled correction was detected; Opus still moved with the signs beyond its retest noise, Haiku partly corrected, and Sonnet's apparent effect rests largely on one pair.
- **Compared with the small nets.** The small nets' sign dependence follows a source's overall error direction but was not the registered proportional mean-error correction (E28), and their inputs carry no meaning. The LLMs' unstated-framing dependence has the form of a bias correction. That the two arise from different mechanisms (a prior learned from text, against a failure to learn an invariance from data) is a hypothesis this design does not test.
- **For M2 (pretrained LLMs).** The posterior's sign invariance was not respected by single-pass answers in these models, as it was not by the small nets. Whether reasoning removes the dependence was not tested with these models and manipulations (E18 used other model versions and big-miss pairs).
- **Limits.** 60 pairs; single-pass answers are noisy (retest variance 0.004-0.73); one negated source per pair, chosen by largest |mean error|; displayed numbers are rounded; specific model versions; Qwen3-1.7B is too inaccurate to interpret.

## Update 55 (2026-10-30 09:13Z): E44, hybrid initialisations: block 1's attention weights had the highest transfer of the solution type; block 2's attention the lowest (amendment 52)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** Six A/B parent pairs, (0, 4), (1, 5), (2, 7), (6, 9), (0, 10), (1, 11) (E37's ctrl seeds). For each pair and each of six weight groups (input embedding; block-1 attention; block-1 MLP; block-2 attention; block-2 MLP; output head), two hybrids: one parent's initialisation with that group from the other parent, trained on the recipient's episode stream (fixed 90,000-step schedule, ctrl format). 72 trainings on two on-demand L4s (1.98 h and 1.97 h, about $3.43). T(G) = the share of acquired hybrids whose final type (middle-range rom sign) equals the donor parent's.
- **P185 holds at its bar; P186 fails.** Block-1 attention had the highest observed transfer, not block-2 attention (intervals corrected after review, see below):
  - Block-1 attention (qkv and output projection, 4,224 of the net's 18,732 parameters): T = 0.75 [0.42, 1.00] (9 of 12; A donors made A in 4 of 6, B donors made B in 5 of 6). Its hybrids' deviations from the Bayes mean correlate more with the donor parent's (median 0.57) than with the recipient's (0.34).
  - Output head: T = 0.73 [0.55, 0.92] (8 of 11; B donors made B in 5 of 5, A donors made A in 3 of 6); median similarity 0.36 to the donor and 0.34 to the recipient. The head's transfer is close to block-1 attention's; no test separates them.
  - Block-2 attention: T = 0.18 [0.00, 0.36]; input embedding 0.30 [0.08, 0.56]; block-1 MLP 0.36 [0.08, 0.67]; block-2 MLP 0.27 [0.00, 0.60]. These hybrids correlate more with their recipient (medians 0.50-0.73) than with their donor (0.31-0.34).
- **An asymmetry (post hoc, descriptive).** A recipients given one group from a B parent became B in 3/6 (input embedding), 5/6 (block-1 attention), 3/6 (block-1 MLP), 2/6 (block-2 attention), 2/5 (block-2 MLP) and 5/5 (head). B recipients became A in 4 of 6 with block-1 attention and 3 of 6 with the head, and once each with the block-1 MLP (recipient 9, donor 6) and the block-2 MLP (recipient 4, donor 0); with the other groups 0. The A recipients were more susceptible to change in these samples.
- **Stalls.** 6 of 72 hybrids did not acquire (input embedding 2, block-1 MLP 1, block-2 attention 1, block-2 MLP 1, head 1).
- **What it shows.** Among single-group swaps in these backgrounds, block 1's initial attention weights went most often with the type and with a donor-like deviation pattern. That is the step where a source's labelled tokens are pooled into its summary (E24-E25 located the big-miss contrast there; E36 found the source summary the most aligned route of the sign shift). Block 2's attention, whose learned routing separates the types in trained nets (E34), had low transfer at initialisation. That block 1 sets up what block 2 learns is a hypothesis; single-group swaps show effects in these backgrounds, not necessity or mediation.

  - the registered bootstrap code turned resampled pairs into a set and dropped multiplicities; corrected in `e44_summ.py` (logged in `prereg_hashes.txt`) and every interval regenerated (point estimates unchanged); the pairs share A parents;
  - state the result as the highest observed transfer in these backgrounds, without necessity or mediation claims, and note that the head is nearly as high;
  - correct the asymmetry (two B-to-A exceptions with MLP groups) and report the conditional counts;
  - describe the similarities as descriptive correlations.

## Update 58 (2026-10-30 11:37Z): E48, supplying the even per-token statistic matches removing the signs, but making it linear gains nothing more; at D = 2 three formats reach similar KL (amendment 56)

**TL;DR**
- **Design.** A 2x2 of input formats in both worlds: the signs of the per-token values present or removed, crossed with the posterior's per-token sufficient statistics given linearly or not. 72 new trainings on three L4 VMs, fixed 90,000-step schedule, seeds 0-11, the same episodes as the comparison arms of each seed:
  - world 1: sq (labelled readings y + r^2; the initialisation of E37's ctrl and mag nets) and sgnsq (ctrl's signed readings plus a feature r^2 on labelled tokens; the initialisation of E39's sgp nets, which carry |r| instead);
  - world 2, D = 2 and D = 1: prod (context tokens carry only the per-example products x_a x_b, x_a y, y^2) and sgnprod (ctrl's [x, y] plus the same products), starting from identical weights equal to ctrl's in every shared parameter.
  Comparison arms: E37's ctrl and mag and E39's sgp (world 1); E40's ctrl and canon (world 2).
- **World 2, D = 2: three formats end at similar mean KL, half of ctrl's.** canon 0.0092, prod 0.0092 and sgnprod 0.0092 nats (ctrl 0.0187); r(prod/canon) = 1.00 [0.91, 1.10] and r(sgnprod/prod) = 1.00 [0.95, 1.07], so differences of about 10% are not excluded; the three are also close at every noise level. With the products given, the measured sign-flip reduction is small: 3.2% of sgnprod's KL, against ctrl's 34.1%.
- **World 2, D = 1: no format moves far from ctrl's 0.0032.** canon 0.0033, prod 0.0029, sgnprod 0.0027; r(prod/canon) = 0.89 [0.73, 1.06]; sgnprod against canon 0.82 [0.73, 0.91]; sgnprod's sign-flip reduction 2.2% (ctrl 32.4%).
- **World 1: r^2 in the reading slot does worse than |r|; as an extra feature it does about as well as |r| on the acquired A-type nets.**
  - sq (all 12 acquired; 2 B): mean KL 0.0100 against mag's 0.0055, r(sq/mag) = 1.81 [1.02, 3.31]; sq is worse than mag at all 11 seeds where mag is A (post hoc). Its big-miss departure is ctrl's size: large-range rom 0.130, against mag's 0.073 and ctrl's 0.133.
  - sgnsq (10 acquired; seeds 5 and 7 stalled; seed 2 B): mean KL 0.0059; sign-flip reduction 1.5% against ctrl's 20.0%; r(sgnsq/sgp) = 0.76 [0.44, 1.06] (9 seeds). Under paired weights and episode streams, its failures overlap with E39's sgp: seeds 5 and 7 stall in both and seed 2 is B in both, while seed 1 stalls only as sgp and seed 3 is B as sgp and A as sgnsq.
- **Predictions: P193 fails, P194 holds, P195 fails, P196 fails, P197 holds on its point estimate** (r(sgnsq/sq) = 0.66 [0.35, 1.26]; the upper limit exceeds the bar of 1.25). The registered account (A-lin: a format's gain is set by how linearly it delivers the per-token statistics) fails as a quantitative account. Linearity added nothing beyond the sign-free fold in world 2, and in world 1 the linear r^2 did worse than |r|. Its second part holds: once the even per-token information is supplied, the measured sign-flip reductions are small.
- **Post hoc, on identical base episodes with the same estimator (as E40's check), against the ctrl nets' sign-averaged predictor.** At D = 2, canon, prod and sgnprod are below it in 8, 11 and 10 of 12 seeds; in world 1 mag is below it in 11 of 11 (sq in 7); at D = 1 the formats are below it in only 1-2 of 12 seeds (sign-averaged ctrl 0.0019; formats 0.0023-0.0029).
- **What it shows (under this recipe, 12 seeds per arm).** The signed format's excess over the sign-free format appears in world 1 and at D = 2, not at D = 1. Where it appears, supplying the even statistic next to the signs gave similar KL to removing the signs: at D = 2 on all seeds, in world 1 on the acquired A-type nets, with stalls and B nets on some seeds. Making the statistic linear added nothing in these tests, and a heavy-tailed linear input (r^2) in world 1's reading slot did worse and kept the full big-miss departure. Two hypotheses fit and are not tested here. First, the excess is the cost of computing even per-token information from signed values. Second, LayerNorm caps large per-token values (E20), which would explain the r^2 result. The measured sign cost (geometric averaging over sign patterns) is a different quantity from the retraining gain: at D = 1 no single trained invariant net reached the averaged ctrl predictor, while at D = 2 and in world 1 the sign-free nets beat it. That is one consistent reading of why the measured cost did not predict the format gain across worlds (E30, E40).
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for four fixes, all done (`results/review_e48.md`):
  - describe associations under this recipe and label the mechanism (computing even information from signed values), the cross-world reading and LayerNorm capping as hypotheses; drop the claim that the remaining error lies downstream;
  - put every run's stalls and types first, and say that failures overlap under paired weights and episode streams (initialisation is not isolated); report P197's interval above its bar;
  - say "similar" rather than "exactly equal", and "small measured sign-flip reduction" rather than "barely used";
  - correct two transcriptions (sgnprod/ctrl lower limit 0.41; the a and c VMs' durations).
  It confirmed the formats and the query token, prod's flip invariance, the pairing and streams, the evaluator routing, the acquisition rules, the bootstrap with multiplicities, P193-P197 as scored, and the identical-episode post hoc comparison.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

At D = 1 the signed nets show no excess over the sign-free and supplied formats, although averaging over sign patterns improves them by a third. A hypothesis that fits, untested: the excess is the cost of computing even per-token information from signed values, and the ctrl nets' sign dependence goes with that computation.
- **Linearity did not matter in these tests.** Products instead of the fold (D = 2: similar KL) and r^2 instead of |r| (world 1: worse in the reading slot, similar as an extra feature) added nothing. The registered quantitative account fails. Where the remaining KL arises is not tested here: the pooling, the computation from the pooled statistics, the output head and the training budget are all candidates.
- **A pointer to LayerNorm, as a hypothesis.** r^2 is heavy-tailed (a big miss gives a large value). In the reading slot it did worse than |r| at every seed where mag is A, and kept ctrl's big-miss departure. That fits E20's account, in which LayerNorm caps per-token evidence so that a big miss counts for less than its square. The same input column also carries the summary tokens' signed readings, so a scale conflict in that column is an alternative; E48 does not separate them.
- **For M2.** Across two tasks, building an invariance into the input helped where the trained net with the nuisance input paid an excess. Supplying the invariant quantity alongside the nuisance helped about as much. The measured invariance cost of a trained net did not predict the gain, because it also contains an averaging effect (D = 1).
- **Limits.** One recipe and width; 12 seeds per arm; world 1's comparisons with sgnsq rest on 9-10 seeds, and its A-type comparisons are survivor-selected; the D = 1 differences are within a few tens of percent; the post hoc table uses other episodes than the test set; the sign share is a finite-ensemble averaging gain, not a measure of how much computation uses the signs; the A/B diagnostic's meaning varies with the format (E30).

## Update 60 (2026-10-30 13:04Z): E51, the nets' sign-induced shifts in the predictive mean are mostly net-specific, and at D = 1 the sign-averaging gain is smaller than a 9-net ensemble's (amendment 59)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (CPU, existing nets).** For the signed ctrl nets of three settings, the predictive mean on each member of a sign family that Bayes ignores (the base and 8 sign-flip patterns): world 1, E37's 11 acquired ctrl nets on E27's first 3,000 bases (flip_ind family); world 2, E40's 12 ctrl nets per D on E40's 6,000 cost episodes and its 8 per-example flip patterns. Measures:
  - rho_h, the mean pairwise correlation across nets of each net's sign-induced shift in the predictive mean (its mean on a member minus its mean over the 9 members);
  - c_sign, the KL reduction of averaging a net over its 9 members (normalised geometric mean; pooled share);
  - c_seed, the same reduction for the normalised geometric mean of 9 different nets of one format on the base input (5 random 9-subsets), for ctrl and for the invariant formats (E37's mag; E40's canon and E48's prod). One estimator per world, as before.
- **P204 fails narrowly: at D = 1 the shifts correlate 0.24 [0.19, 0.30] across nets** (bar <= 0.2; jackknife interval over nets, see the review). In world 1 the correlation is 0.14 [0.09, 0.20], at D = 2 0.28 [0.19, 0.36]. In the predictive mean the sign-induced shifts are mostly net-specific, with a modest shared part. Whether shared sign effects exist in other aspects of the predictive density was not measured.
- **P205 holds: at D = 1, averaging 9 canon nets reduces their KL by 43%, more than averaging one ctrl net over sign patterns (32%).** The bar was 0.75 x 0.32. As a benchmark, the sign-averaged ctrl net's advantage over every trained invariant net at D = 1 (E48) is smaller than the gain of this ensemble of invariant nets, which is compatible with an ensemble reading of the sign-averaging gain.
- **Ensembles over seeds (descriptive).** 9-net geometric ensembles reduce the mean KL by 36-55% in every format and setting: world 1, ctrl 0.0132 to 0.0059 and mag 0.0061 to 0.0034; D = 1, ctrl 0.0028 to 0.0015, canon 0.0028 to 0.0016, prod 0.0022 to 0.0013; D = 2, ctrl 0.0184 to 0.0104, canon 0.0088 to 0.0056, prod 0.0081 to 0.0047. The nets' sign-averaged deviations from the Bayes mean correlate 0.47 (world 1), 0.69 (D = 1) and 0.68 (D = 2) across nets: their mean errors are largely shared, their sign-induced mean shifts are not.
- **Post hoc, model-based split.** Under KL(M) = K_shared + K_specific / M for M-net geometric means, fitted to two ensemble sizes, the net-specific part is about 40-62% of the mean single-net KL in every setting and format. Where the signed format pays an excess (E48), the estimates put it in both parts. World 1: shared, ctrl 0.0050 against mag 0.0030; specific, 0.0082 against 0.0030. D = 2: shared, ctrl 0.0094 against canon 0.0052 and prod 0.0042; specific, 0.0089 against 0.0035 and 0.0039. These are conditional estimates without uncertainty or a test of the model.
- **What it shows.** In the predictive mean, the shift a ctrl net makes under a sign flip is mostly its own. Averaging one net over sign patterns gained less than averaging 9 independently trained nets of an invariant format. This is compatible with reading the sign cost measured since E27 largely as net-specific variation under a nuisance transformation, and that reading would explain why it did not predict the retraining gain (E30, E40, E48); E51 does not establish it. About half of a single net's mean KL is removed by averaging 9 nets in every format tried.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e51.md`):
  - restrict the finding to predictive-mean shifts and call the ensemble reading compatible, not established; drop causal explanations of earlier results; note that an architecture-level account could also predict the distribution of net-specific errors;
  - the registered resampling for rho_h dropped repeated nets (a subsampling); replaced by a leave-one-net-out jackknife interval (`e51_summ.py`, logged in `prereg_hashes.txt`; point estimates and P204-P205 unchanged);
  - label the split as model-based conditional estimates of mean KL, without claims of equality between formats;
  - note that the ensemble-mean variance ratio includes a 1/N floor (0.08-0.09);
  - describe the seed-ensemble comparison as a benchmark between specific geometric averages.
  It confirmed the families, nets, grids and estimators, the point formulas, the P204-P205 scoring, the hashes and the disclosed plumbing order.

**What this says.**
- **Width, signed format.** From width 32 to 128 the single-net KL and the 9-net ensemble KL of ctrl nets both fall to about 0.53-0.54 of their width-32 values, and the share removed by averaging stays near 0.53-0.56. In this cohort and range, the part shared across trainings is not a fixed component that width leaves behind. Whether a smaller fixed component exists, and whether the shrinkage reflects the architecture or the optimisation, is not separated. E38's finding that the signed format's relative cost persists at width 128 is consistent: the structure of the departure persists while its size shrinks.
- **Width, sign-free format.** mag's varying part fell more than its shared part at width 128, and width 64 was worse because of three B nets, so the picture is not uniform across formats.
- **Depth.** A third block mainly lowered the shared part (the 9-net ensemble reaches width 128's level) while the varying part fell only slightly, so single depth-3 nets are limited relatively more by what varies between trainings. This fits E17's and E38's partial depth effects.
- **For M2.** For the signed format, up to width 128, the departure behaves as a capacity effect in both of its parts, with a stable ratio between them. An account that predicts the departure from the architecture would need to predict how it scales with size; three widths are too few to fit a scaling law, and a smaller fixed component is not excluded.
- **Limits.** Existing nets, 10-12 per cell; one recipe and world; the shared/varying split rests on E51's two-point model; ensembles overlap across subsets, and subset ranges are not population intervals; width 64's mag cell includes three B nets.

## Update 63 (2026-10-30 15:36Z): E54, world 2 shows no general under-count of a concentrated residual; the direction depends on the format and D (amendment 62)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (CPU, existing nets).** World-2 matched contexts: for 4,000 base episodes per D (D = 1, 2; N = 8; seeds 54,001-2), two versions with the same X^T X, X^T y and y.y, so exact Bayes is identical (checked to 2e-13): the least-squares residual concentrated on one example (median largest share 0.93 at D = 1, 0.80 at D = 2) or spread (0.23, 0.31). The two recipes also differ in the residual's direction, signs and which example carries it (drawn independently), so the contrast is between two residual-generation recipes with the same sufficient statistics, not concentration alone. All 120 world-2 nets (E40 ctrl and canon, E48 prod and sgnprod, E49 pre; 12 per arm and D). dls = mean log-sd of the predictive, concentrated minus spread (< 0: narrower, the concentrated residual under-counted in the scale); lam = how far the mean moves along the leave-the-outlier-out fit (> 0: the outlier discounted).
- **P212 fails.** ctrl nets at D = 2: dls -0.012 [-0.017, -0.007], narrower in 12 of 12; at D = 1: +0.006 [-0.001, +0.015], narrower in 5 of 12.
- **P213 fails.** lam at D = 2: 0.030 [0.023, 0.037], 12 of 12 positive; at D = 1: 0.014 [-0.005, 0.031], 8 of 12.
- **P214 fails: mean dls < 0 in 3 of 10 arms** (ctrl and pre at D = 2; pre at D = 1 at -0.0004). The product formats widen (+0.012 to +0.028; none of their 48 nets narrower) and canon widens (+0.012, +0.006), while the products' mean still moves as if the outlier were discounted (prod, D = 1: lam 0.061, 12 of 12). Aggregate effects are small: geometric SD ratios from about -1.2% to +2.9%. On the calibration versions, the effects lie between about 10% of RSS over-counted (sgnprod, D = 2) and 4% under-counted (ctrl, D = 2). The concentrated versions cost more KL than the spread ones in every arm (0.002-0.007 nats).
- **Post hoc (`e54_post.py`, not registered): an association with the episode's scale, not an identified size effect.** Pooled by RSS quartile, dls is lower in the top quartile than in the bottom one in all 120 nets, and its top-quartile mean is negative in 8 of 10 arms. But RSS quartiles also differ in noise level and in the scale of y, and within a true noise level the difference between larger and smaller RSS is inconsistent: at the lowest level larger RSS goes with more widening in 9 of 10 arms; at the highest level the sign varies by arm. lam is larger in the upper half of RSS than in the lower half in 9 of 10 arms (from negative to positive in 7), with the same confound.
- **What it shows.** The registered account, a general bias of these transformers toward under-counting a concentrated deviation in what they pool, fails in world 2: its direction depends on the input format and D, and the effects are small. World 1's big-miss departure is therefore not a property shared by every net and format of the two tasks. The post hoc associations with the episode's scale do not identify a mechanism.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for four fixes, all done (`results/review_e54.md`):
  - the RSS split mixes noise levels and y scales, so the faster-than-square-then-saturating account and the parallel with world 1 are not identified; within-level comparisons added (`e54_post.py`), which do not support a size effect; the account was removed;
  - "narrower as RSS grows" overstated monotonicity (only the top-against-bottom quartile comparison holds in all 120 nets); reworded;
  - the two versions differ in residual direction, signs and the outlier's position as well as concentration; described as two recipes;
  - the 1-5% range mixed aggregate and quartile effects; aggregate SD ratios are -1.2% to +2.9%.
  It confirmed the sufficient-statistic and Bayes invariance, the 120 loaders and formats, the moments, the KL direction, the registered dls, lam and u and the bootstrap with multiplicities, the tables and JSON, and P212-P214's failures.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.

**What this says.**

One bias of these transformers toward under-counting a concentrated deviation, whatever the format, is ruled out in world 2.
- **No identified size effect (post hoc).** The pooled quartiles suggested that the direction switches with the residual's size, but within a noise level the relation is inconsistent and at the lowest level runs the other way in most arms, so the quartile pattern reflects differences in noise level and in the scale of y. Whether the direction depends on the deviation's size at a fixed noise level would need a registered scale sweep.
- **For M2 (across tasks).** The big-miss departure, the program's lead fingerprint in world 1 (present in every acquired net and format there), has no consistent counterpart in world 2: its direction there depends on the input format and D, and its size is small. An account of the departure must therefore be specific about what the nets pool in each task (in world 1, directly visible per-source errors; in world 2, raw examples or products), not a general property of attention pooling.

## Update 64 (2026-10-30 16:45Z): E57, the LayerNorm cap scale separates the A/B types strongly only from 20,000-40,000 steps, later than the routing markers; its median falls during acquisition and rises afterwards (amendment 65)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (CPU, checkpoint weights).** For E47's 215 acquired lineages with a known final type (142 B; E37's ctrl runs, E43's branches and new initialisations, E44's hybrids, E46's perturbed runs; clusters = parent seeds), the cap scale c of block 1's LayerNorm (`lngeom.py`, as E55: c = A / U, the median over labelled tokens of the norm of the token's error-free part over the norm of the error direction in the input embedding) at 10 checkpoints from step 0 to 90,000. AUC_c = P(c of a final-A lineage > c of a final-B lineage), 2,000 cluster-bootstrap resamples; E47's duplicate rule for E43 branches.
- **P222 holds on its point estimate.** AUC_c at step 0: 0.51 [0.38, 0.65] (median c 2.07 in A, 2.06 in B); the interval extends beyond [0.4, 0.6], so absence of information at initialisation is not established.
- **P223 holds on its point estimate.** AUC_c at 10,000 steps 0.66 [0.54, 0.79] (the interval crosses 0.75), when E47's block-1 cross-source attention and sign-cost share separate the types at 0.97.
- **P224 holds: strong separation by 40,000 steps.** AUC_c 0.96 [0.94, 0.99]; 0.90 at 20,000, 0.98 at 60,000 and 80,000, 0.94 at the end (median c 4.21 in A, 3.70 in B). Leaving out E37's lineages changes no AUC by more than 0.013 (not an independent replication).
- **A common time course of the group medians (descriptive).** The median c falls from 2.07 (A) and 2.06 (B) at initialisation to 1.33-1.44 at 2,000-3,000 steps, the window in which reliability weighting and the departure appear (E16: onset at 2,500-2,750 steps in two replays, peaks at 4,500 and 9,000), and then rises at every later sampled step (A: 1.53 at 5,000, 2.84 at 20,000, 4.21 at 90,000; B: 1.52, 2.53, 3.70). Individual lineages need not rise monotonically (E37 ctrl seed 8 falls from 1.27 to 1.22 between 3,000 and 5,000). At 2,000 steps the order is reversed (AUC_c 0.30 [0.14, 0.44]: B lineages have the higher c).
- **Post-review diagnostics (`e57_post.py`, not registered).** c's one-parameter reading assumes a narrow spread of the error-free norm A and a small cross term rho. At initialisation both are large (A's coefficient of variation 0.27, median |rho| 0.35); from 2,000 steps on they are 0.11-0.17 and 0.05-0.15. The later rise of c comes mostly from A (median 0.98 at 5,000 steps to 2.73 at 90,000 in A lineages, 0.99 to 2.58 in B), while U stays between 0.58 and 0.76; at the end B lineages have both a smaller A and a larger U.
- **What it shows.** The end-of-training difference in the cap scale between the types (E55's association) is not detected at initialisation on the point estimate, is reversed at 2,000 steps, and discriminates strongly in its final direction only from 20,000-40,000 steps, later than E47's routing markers. That the B type's smaller cap scale is a consequence of its route is a hypothesis this ordering is consistent with but does not test. The group medians describe a two-phase time course of the cap scale: a fall during acquisition, then a rise driven mostly by the error-free part of the embedding; with E55's within-run link between c and the departure, a reading of this rise as gradual un-capping that shrinks the departure is a hypothesis for testing on behaviour at these checkpoints.

Everything else trained from the seed's usual initialisation on the usual episodes (fixed 90,000-step schedule, seeds 0-5): E53's uniform factorised pool (unif) at c = 1, 2, 4 and the baseline learned pool at c = 1, 4. 30 trainings on one L4 (1.77 h, $1.54; lane GPU total $33.58 of $40). Constrained-Bayes values at these c from amendment 63's table.
- **P225 holds: the departure lies close to constrained Bayes at the designed cap scale.** rom_large 0.222 [0.216, 0.228], 0.117 [0.113, 0.120], 0.039 [0.038, 0.040] at c = 1, 2, 4 (constrained Bayes 0.211, 0.107, 0.033); rom_middle 0.179, 0.054, 0.017 (0.176, 0.053, 0.014). Every arm is within 0.011 of the prediction (bar 0.03), the fall is monotone and sixfold, and the 18 nets lie within 0.02 of their arm's mean in the large range. The large-range predictions lie below every arm's seed interval (excess 0.006-0.011), so this is agreement within the registered tolerance, not an exact prediction; the constrained-Bayes values are simulated (stable to 0.0003 across draws, bins and seeds; `/tmp/s6/cb_robust.py`).

With the same frozen embedding the learned-pool nets learned poorly: at c = 1, 5 of 6 met the acquisition rule at KL 0.063-0.073 (about five times ctrl's 0.0127); at c = 4, 4 of 6 stalled and the two others ended at 0.078 and 0.085. That these nets were too far from a working solution for the test to bear on standard learned pools is a post hoc reading.

The rescaling also changes the signed normalised feature, and the pool keeps a vector, so the even-only reader is an approximation, not the identified bottleneck. For learned pools the registered prediction failed, and the cap's role there remains an association (E55). With E50 (a departure without LayerNorm under learned weighting), two routes to the departure, the cap and the learned weighting, remain a hypothesis.

## Update 67 (2026-10-30 20:29Z): E55, the LayerNorm cap scale read from the input embedding predicts the uniform-pool nets' departure through constrained Bayes (P215); with learned pools it orders the departure within cohorts, rises during training as the departure decays, and is larger at width 128 (P216-P218) (amendment 63)

**TL;DR**
- **Design (CPU, weights and existing evaluations).** The cap scale c of block 1's LayerNorm (`lngeom.py`): with a labelled token's centred embedding a_i + r_i u~, LayerNorm divides by sqrt(A^2 + 2 r A U rho + r^2 U^2), so a uniform mean of token values carries the even feature 1 - (1 + r^2 / c^2)^(-1/2) with c = A / U (median over the labelled tokens of E27's first 500 bases, from inp.weight and inp.bias only). A constrained-Bayes reader of that feature gives, on E12's pairs, a departure fixed by c (table in `results/e55_cbtable.json`). Cohorts: E53's uniform-pool nets (seeds 1-11, prospective), 23 confirmatory learned-pool cohorts (E38, E30 fix, E48 sq, E43, E44, E46), E37's runs over training; E37's final nets were the exploration.
- **P215 holds (uniform pools, approximate quantitative agreement).** For E53's uni and unif nets of seeds 1-11 (seed 0 explored), the mean measured departure against the mean constrained-Bayes value at each net's c: uni rom_large 0.171 against 0.164, rom_middle 0.102 against 0.101; unif 0.177 against 0.166, 0.106 against 0.104 (bar 0.03). The large-range values are 0.007-0.010 above the prediction, as in E58. These nets learned nearly the same cap scale (c 1.36-1.45; A's coefficient of variation 0.008; |rho| 0.005), so the test is of arm means near c = 1.4; within-arm correlations are uninformative, and the even-only reader is an approximation, not an identified scalar bottleneck.
- **P216 holds (learned pools, an association across related cohorts).** Within-cohort Spearman correlation of c with rom_large negative in 21 of 23 registered confirmatory cohorts, median -0.75 (exceptions: mag at depth 3 +0.16 and at width 128 +0.38). A naming error had left out E44's input-embedding group (12 nets; the registered text named all six groups); with it, 22 of 24, median -0.75 (that group: -0.70; correction logged). E43's, E44's and E46's cohorts share parents with the exploration cohort, so this is a registered descriptive score, not independent replications. The measured departure differs from the constrained-Bayes value at these nets' c (E43's cohorts 0.13 against 0.045; E38 width-128 mag -0.002 against 0.025): a model mismatch for learned pools.
- **P217 holds.** Median c at width 128 against width 32: ctrl 4.47 against 3.79; mag 4.71 against 4.63 (mag barely).
- **P218 holds (after a disclosed correction).** Within E37's 23 acquired pure runs, Spearman(c, rom_large) over the measured checkpoints from 6,000 to 90,000 steps is negative in 22, median -0.93 (c rises from 1.3-2.5 to 3.5-4.9 in most runs while rom_large falls from 0.22-0.44 to 0.03-0.16); ctrl seed 8, the worst B net, ends at c 1.62 and rom_large 0.194; the exception is the B-type mag seed 3, whose c stays low and whose departure rises. The registered code included checkpoints where the trajectory's rom is not measured (NaN); corrected and logged; the registered output is kept.
- **The cap's cost (descriptive).** A constrained-Bayes reader of the even capped feature loses 0.0022 nats at c = 1, 0.0009 at 1.4, 0.0003 at 2, 0.00008 at 3 and 0.00003 at 4 (quadrature, 4,000 test episodes); this is the simulated reader's cost, not the gain available to a trained net.
- **The tension with E50 and E58 (coordinator's note).** E50 found that the departure survives removing block 1's LayerNorm in the ctrl and sq formats (halving only with |r|), so the cap is not necessary for a departure in learned-pool nets. E58 showed that with a uniform pool, setting c by design changes the departure by about the constrained-Bayes amount; its test for learned pools failed (P226; those nets learned poorly, a post hoc limitation on generalising). So c is a cause of the departure where the pool is uniform (in E58's design) and a correlate where it is learned; what else produces the learned-pool nets' departure (the learned weighting, later stages) is open.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for five fixes, all done (`results/review_e55.md`):
  - the gap between the measured departure and the constrained-Bayes value cannot be read as a share caused elsewhere, and the threefold description fails in one cohort: reworded as a model mismatch, attention one hypothesis;
  - E58's learned-pool test failed and is kept as a failure, with poor learning as a post hoc limitation;
  - the even-only reader is an approximation (arm-level agreement near c = 1.4), and the cap's KL cost is the simulated reader's, not the nets' available gain;
  - the confirmatory cohorts are related to the exploration cohort: described as a registered descriptive score;
  - table corrections (E44's groups: the input-embedding group had been left out by a naming error, now included and logged; P216's median -0.75; ctrl seed 8's endpoint; E53's rows include seed 0; the sq cohort's constrained-Bayes value is not meaningful).
  It confirmed the A / U computation, the interpolation, acquisition and exclusions, P215-P217's scores and the corrected P218, and the hashes and correction log.

| P218 | within E37's runs, Spearman(c, rom_large) over checkpoints >= 5,000 steps negative in >= 80% | holds (after the NaN correction): 22 of 23, median -0.93 |

**What this says.**
- **One geometric number of the first layer, two relations to the departure.** Where the pool is uniform, the arm-mean departure agrees approximately with the constrained-Bayes departure of LayerNorm's even capped feature at the cap scale read from the weights (P215; the causal version is E58). Where the pool is learned, the same number orders the departure across related nets and over training (P216, P218), but the constrained-Bayes model does not match its size (larger than predicted in most cohorts), so for these nets c is a correlate, not an established cause, and the model mismatch is unexplained; the learned weighting (E50, E53) is one hypothesis.
- **Why the departure persists (a hypothesis).** At the cap scale learned-pool nets reach (about 3.8-4.7), the cap itself costs a Bayes-optimal reader about 0.00003-0.00004 nats, about 0.3% of a ctrl net's KL, so raising c further gains almost nothing; the uniform-pool nets keep c near 1.4, where the cap costs about 0.0009 nats. Whether this weak incentive is why c stops rising is not tested.
- **Width and training (associations).** c is larger at width 128 than at width 32 (barely for mag) and rises within runs while the departure decays, which fits the departure's shrinkage with width and training (E38, E16) but does not establish the cause.
- **The tension with E50.** Without block 1's LayerNorm the learned-pool nets still show the departure (E50), so the cap is not necessary for it there; E58 found the cap causal with a uniform pool, and its learned-pool test failed. Two routes, the cap and something else (the learned weighting or later stages), remain a hypothesis for the standard nets.
- **Limits.** c is a median of a geometric ratio whose one-parameter reading needs a narrow A and a small rho (true for the uniform-pool nets, approximately for trained learned-pool nets, not at initialisation; E57); the constrained-Bayes reader uses only the even feature; cohorts are clustered (E43, E44 and E46 share parents with the exploration cohort); the uniform-pool test is at the arm level.

**What this says.**
- **Membership, not fixed weights (measured endpoints).** Told which four tokens belong to the source, a learned pool is as close to Bayes as the uniform pool (KL within about 5%, slightly closer) with a small sign share; so the uniform architecture's KL advantage is the advantage of given membership. Its code dependence and run-to-run variation were not measured here. The registered account, that the learned within-source weighting makes the cost, fails.
- **A much smaller departure with learned weights and given membership.** The learned restricted pool takes the departure from the uniform pool's 0.17 to 0.018 (and to the A pattern at middle errors), much further than the standard nets (0.13). That this happens as in E20's toy (an attention pool weighting larger errors up undoes the cap) is a hypothesis; the weights, values and cap geometry of these nets were not analysed.
- **One attention, two jobs (a hypothesis).** In the standard nets block 1's attention must both find a source's tokens among all fifteen by their arbitrary codes and weight them by their errors. A reading that fits E53-E60 is that doing both in one step costs most of the KL and leaves the cap only partly corrected; E60 shows the effect of handing over membership, not the mechanism of any interference.
- **For M2 (explain the inductive bias).** Under this recipe, handing the nets a source's membership removes most of the standard architecture's excess KL over the uniform pool's level and, with learned weights, most of the departure; content-based routing (finding a group's members from arbitrary identity codes) is therefore the leading candidate for the main inductive-bias cost in this task, not an identified mechanism.
- **Limits.** One recipe and width; 12 (own) and 8 (ownf) seeds; four ctrl seeds for the device check; the restricted pool hard-codes membership, which says what membership is worth, not how standard nets could find it better; sign shares are geometric-averaging gains.

**TL;DR**
- **Design (CPU, existing nets).** Block 1 of the summary tokens (4, 9, 14) on E27's first 2,000 bases. Cohorts: ctrl (E37's 11 acquired ctrl nets), fix (E30's 12 fixed-code nets), own (E60's 12 nets told the membership), ext (199 acquired final nets of E43, E44 and E46, the five explored nets excluded; 11 parent clusters) and traj (E37's 11 ctrl runs at 10 checkpoints). Measures: per head, the mass on the source's own labelled tokens (P_h; pooling head: >= 0.5) and on the three query-question tokens (C_h; "consensus" head: >= 0.5, a mass criterion, not a function); the pre-LN logit decomposition logit_j = (alpha_j + beta r_j) / n_j + const (exact up to LayerNorm's eps: relative denominator error below 5e-5 on these tokens), giving the norm-scaled own logit L_own = alpha / A, the norm term's contribution at |r| = 3 (dlogit) and the signed numerator's coefficient K_odd; leakage; the per-source LayerNorm norm A; KL with idealised source codes at evaluation.
- **P237 fails: consensus head and type agree in all 11 ctrl nets but not in fix.** Every ctrl B net has a consensus head (C_max 0.98-0.99) and no A net does (0.00); in fix, 5 of 8 B nets have none (their non-pooling heads put most of their mass on other sources' labelled tokens or spread it).
- **P238 holds.** Over ext, AUC(C_max; B > A) 1.00 [1.00, 1.00]: a consensus head in 129 of 132 B nets and in none of 67 A nets.
- **Post hoc: two pooling heads if and only if A, in all 222 nets** (ctrl, fix, ext); 15 B nets have no pooling head (1 ctrl, 5 fix, 9 ext). Of the B nets' non-pooling heads in the random-code cohorts, 137 of 149 are consensus heads.
- **Over training (traj, descriptive).** At 2,000 steps every run has a head with C_max >= 0.62 and almost none has a pooling head; the first pooling head appears between 2,000 and 5,000 steps (never in s8, the worst B net); the A runs' second pooling head appears at 5,000 (s1), 10,000 (s0, s2) or 20,000 steps (s6), while every B run keeps its consensus head (0.93-0.99 from 5,000 steps on). AUC 0.93 at 2,000 steps, 1.00 from 10,000.
- **P239 holds.** In all 8 A nets with two pooling heads (4 ctrl, 4 fix), the two heads' mean K_odd have opposite signs (e.g. ctrl s0: +1.41 and -2.19); so do all 12 own nets' heads. This is a sign pattern of one logit coefficient; with unequal value and output maps it does not by itself establish cancellation of the sign dependence.
- **P240 holds.** (a) All 14 ctrl pooling heads have L_own 14-22 and dlogit -2.9 to -4.2: the norm term alone lowers an own key's unnormalised score at |r| = 3 by about 3.5 nats against r = 0. (b) own's median L_own is -0.82 (norm term +0.43 at |r| = 3), against ctrl's 16.8. fix is intermediate (L_own 2.9-5.3; -0.9 to -1.8).
- **P241 holds.** Orthonormal unit source codes at evaluation lower the KL of all 11 ctrl nets, by 14.4% on average (equal norms alone 6%, orthogonality alone 8%); own's changes by 0.1%.
- **Leakage and the code-set normaliser (descriptive).** Pooling heads put 1.0% (A) and 2.5% (B) of their mass on other sources' tokens, heavy-tailed (99% quantile 0.18-0.29), and more when codes overlap (Spearman about +0.47, positive in all 200 random-code nets with a pooling head). The per-source LayerNorm norm A varies by 13-15% (medians) across episodes in ctrl and ext, almost entirely through the codes; 0.65% in own, 0.9-1.4% in fix.
- **What it shows.** (1) The program's two solution types (E6-E57) go with two allocations of the summary's two block-1 heads: two pooling heads (A) or fewer (B), the other head with random codes almost always on the three summaries. Every run starts with such a head; A runs later convert it. (2) A's two pooling heads carry opposite odd coefficients; whether this explains A's smaller sign dependence (E27) is a hypothesis. (3) In pre-LN attention an error's size enters a key's score only through the LayerNorm norm and the signed feature; the standard nets' large positive norm-scaled routing logits lower large errors' scores, which works against correcting the cap, while nets told the membership have slightly negative ones, consistent with their near-zero departure (E60); fixed codes are intermediate. That this is a cause of the departure or the KL is not tested here. (4) Orthonormal codes help the trained standard nets at evaluation (14%). Apart from (4), these are associations and algebraic decompositions, not causal tests.
- **Review:** Codex (GPT-6) asked for six fixes, all done (`results/review_e63.md`):
  - the decomposition omitted LayerNorm's eps: quantified (relative denominator error below 5e-5 on these tokens) and stated;
  - dlogit is the norm term's contribution and K_odd the signed numerator's coefficient, not complete weight effects or a demonstrated cancellation: reworded, the "30 times less weight" replaced by an unnormalised-score factor, the sign pair and the departure link kept as hypotheses;
  - B's allocation was overstated (15 B nets have no pooling head; 137 of 149 counts heads; C is a mass criterion): reworded to "fewer than two pooling heads", post hoc;
  - the claim that the code dependence left after idealisation is not about norms and overlaps compared unlike interventions: deleted;
  - the training timing generalised medians: per-run intervals given;
  - labels and counts: 200 (not 196) leakage correlations, the KL column is the test-NLL gap, A CV aggregates are medians.
  It confirmed the cohorts, filters, exclusions and clusters, the Bayes-invariant Loewdin transformations, the attention definitions, P237's failure and P238-P241's scores.
- **Decision for Kelvin:** none.
